readerTitle: Why 'hire when you're busy' is already too late
caseNote: 가상 사례 (에어컨 수리업체, 일정관리 소프트웨어 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 채용 시점은 지금 얼마나 바쁜지가 아니라, 그 사람이 제 몫을 하게 될 때 수요가 얼마일지로 정한다. 바쁘다고 느낄 때는 이미 리드타임만큼 늦은 것이다.
misconception: 정말 일손이 부족해질 때 뽑아야 돈을 아낀다. 사람을 뽑으면 바로 일손이 늘어난다.

sources.text: 인력 계획의 일반 개념 (채용 리드타임, 신규 인력의 온보딩·램프업 기간)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 가정: 채용 1개월, 입사 첫 달 0%(동행 교육), 둘째 달 50%(40건), 셋째 달부터 100%(월 80건). 성수기는 6~8월.
5번 카드의 직무별 램프업 기간(단순 직무는 며칠~몇 주, 기술직·영업직은 몇 달, 관리자는 더 길다)은 일반적인 경향으로만 적었고 구체 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 업종·국가별로 차이가 큽니다.

cards.title: Why 'hire when you're busy' is already too late
body: You run an air-conditioning repair company. Every June, the phones ring more than your four technicians can handle.
So you hire. It feels careful: you only pay for help once you're sure you need it. But by the time the new tech is truly useful, summer is nearly over.

image.label: Overflowing phone queue while a new technician reads a manual
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 한여름 사무실, 전화기에 대기 통화 표시가 넘쳐나고, 구석에서 새 기술자가 두꺼운 매뉴얼을 읽고 있음. 창밖에 뜨거운 해. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: When should you start looking for a new technician?
body: Your rush runs June to August. Finding a good technician takes about a month. A new hire then spends one month shadowing, one month at half speed, and reaches full speed in month three: about 80 jobs a month.
When do you start the search?

options.text: In June, once the phones overflow
options.feedback: You never pay for help you don't need. But the tech starts in July and adds only about 40 jobs before summer ends.

options.text: In May, a month before the rush
options.feedback: Much better, about 120 summer jobs. But they're still shadowing in June, when you need them most.

options.text: In March, three months before the rush
options.feedback: They hit full speed by June, for about 240 summer jobs. The price is two months of wages before the busy season pays you back.

cards.title: Same person, three start dates.

breakdown.label: Search in June
breakdown.detail: Starts July, half speed in August

breakdown.label: Search in May
breakdown.detail: Starts June, full speed in August

cards.callout: Summer jobs completed by one new technician.

cards.title: Hiring ahead of growth
body: **Hiring ahead of growth** means adding people before the demand arrives, because people take time to find and time to get good.
Count back: the date you need them, minus time to hire, minus time to ramp up. June minus three months is March.
Feeling overloaded is a late signal. When you feel it, you're already behind by your full **lead time**.

image.label: Timeline counting back from June to March
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 인포그래픽. 3월 "Start search", 4월 "Shadowing", 5월 "Half speed", 6~8월 "Full speed" 구간을 색으로 구분. 6월 위에 "Rush begins" 깃발. 3월에서 6월로 이어지는 화살표에 "Lead time: 3 months".

cards.title: Every role has its own lead time.
body: Ramp time also eats your best people's hours, since someone has to train the new hire. Roughly:
list: **Simple roles** like counter staff or movers: days to a few weeks
**Skilled trades** like electricians or technicians: often months
**Sales roles:** months, to learn the product and build a pipeline
**Managers:** longer still, to learn the people and the work
cards.callout: The longer the ramp, the earlier the decision.

cards.title: Hire ahead of evidence, not hope.
body: This works when demand is predictable: a season that repeats every year, a signed contract, a growing backlog of booked work.
Hiring ahead of demand you only hope for is something else. That's premature scaling. The salaries arrive on schedule. The customers may not.

cards.title: Early hires cost real money.
body: Each month of ramp is a month of wages with little output. Hire too far ahead, and cash can run short before demand shows up. Idle new hires also lose energy, and cutting them later hurts the people who stay.
Lower the risk: hire one step ahead, not five. Bridge gaps with overtime or contractors. Tie each next hire to a clear trigger, such as booked work.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your scheduling software just signed its biggest client. Their 2,000 staff will move onto your product over the next three months. A new support rep needs about six weeks before they can answer tickets alone. Your team is busy but coping.

options.text: Wait until the ticket queue grows, then hire
options.feedback: No wasted wages, but new reps arrive weeks after the flood. The new client's first impression is slow replies.

options.text: Hire for the signed contract now, and set a backlog trigger for more
options.feedback: You pay a few weeks of training wages, but reps are ready when users land. The trigger keeps you from hiring on hope.

options.text: Hire six reps now, since sales says more big deals are coming
options.feedback: You'd be ready for anything, but promised deals aren't signed ones. If they slip, you carry six salaries on one contract.

cards.title: Hire for the demand you'll have when they're ready.
body: Time to hire plus time to ramp tells you when to start. Solid evidence of demand tells you whether to start at all.
**Try it today:** pick your next likely hire. Write down how long it takes to find and train them, then count back from when you'll need them.
